claims.text: Combining in situ synchrotron XRD, high-resolution electron microscopy, and a physics-informed machine-learning surrogate will improve prediction accuracy and efficiency for HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated method will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness under tensile and fracture testing.
HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure characterized by multilevel chemical fluctuations.
In situ synchrotron XRD can capture the relevant real-time phase and lattice evolution during tensile and fracture tests.
High-resolution electron microscopy during mechanical loading can capture dynamic microstructural evolution and chemical heterogeneity.
Digital image correlation can provide local strain-field information during room-temperature tensile testing.
A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate will be trained using measured microstructural-evolution and local-strain descriptors.
Testing will be performed at room temperature, optionally at moderately elevated temperatures, under controlled conditions with high temporal resolution.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and localized strain zones mediate phase responses and crack nucleation.
Elasticity and fracture-mechanics constraints combined with dynamic microstructural descriptors will allow the surrogate to predict mechanical properties rapidly.
The surrogate can avoid computationally intensive first-principles and CALPHAD calculations.
The proposed method will reduce mean prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional methods.
The proposed method will increase computational efficiency by approximately three- to five-fold.
Existing approaches rely solely on first-principles calculations, CALPHAD, or standard machine-learning models.
Existing computational approaches are inefficient and have particular difficulty predicting fracture properties.
The model will become unreliable when temporal or spatial resolution is insufficient to resolve rapid microstructural fluctuations, such as at very high strain rates or extreme temperatures.
Prior work on other high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys supports the utility of in situ characterization for resolving chemically heterogeneous mechanical responses.
Prior work supports machine-learning prediction of mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
Experimental noise and integration complexity may reduce reproducibility and alter the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% error reduction and a three- to five-fold efficiency gain relative to traditional methods will falsify the hypothesis.
